title: Tinkering in Primary School: From Episode to Science Practice
venue: The Primary School as a Playful Space
extended_summary:
This paper examines how tinkering, understood as an open-ended constructionist practice, can be integrated into formal primary school science education without losing its exploratory character. The authors are interested in a central tension: tinkering can generate authentic student questions and deep engagement, but teachers often feel unprepared to connect those questions to disciplinary learning, especially in physics.

The study centers on the TIDE model (Tinkering, Ideas generation, Disciplinary connection, Exploration), which the authors developed as a way to bridge tinkering experiences with school curriculum. The implemented project, Oﬃcina della Luce (Light Workshop), ran in four primary schools in Bologna and involved 13 classrooms, 24 teachers, and approximately 300 students. Teachers received professional development in tinkering, access to a resource library of light-related activities, and a documentation protocol using fishbowl discussions; classrooms then carried out multiple light-tinkering workshops, though the original eight-month plan was compressed to four months because of pandemic-related disruption.

The analysis combines questionnaire responses from 20 teachers with qualitative examination of fishbowl documentation. Findings suggest that tinkering helped re-engage students, especially those who struggle in conventional school settings, while also revealing unexpected vulnerabilities among some high-performing, highly school-oriented students. At the same time, teachers reported uneasiness in handling emergent scientific questions and tended to choose humanities, storytelling, or expressive pathways more often than direct science follow-up. The authors conclude that tinkering can be a powerful entry point for student agency and scientific curiosity, but that effective integration into primary science teaching requires stronger disciplinary support for teachers and more sustained documentation of learning over time.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/action-research study with teacher questionnaires, coded open-ended responses, and one fishbowl protocol. It offers rich contextual evidence but no controlled design, randomization, or quantitative causal estimate.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests meaningful classroom-level benefits for engagement and inquiry, especially for students on the margins of school success, but it reports no effect sizes and provides only preliminary, context-specific evidence. The impact is therefore promising but unclear in magnitude.

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that tinkering positively affected classroom dynamics, teacher engagement, and student access to knowledge, based on feedback from 20 teachers and fishbowl protocol analysis. Teachers also reported unexpectedly high engagement and participation among students often seen as disengaged, while some high-performing students experienced frustration or crisis during open-ended tasks.
finding.measure: Teacher questionnaire responses and qualitative fishbowl protocol analysis of classroom documentation
finding.study_size: n=20 teachers; approximately 300 students across 13 primary school classrooms

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that tinkering supported collaboration, self-reflection, mutual assistance, creativity, and student agency, especially in open-ended group work. The paper provides qualitative evidence that students developed persistence in managing frustration and working through failure, though no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher reports coded from open-ended questionnaire responses and classroom documentation

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that tinkering surfaced relevant scientific questions, particularly around the physics of light, and prompted students to formulate and investigate research questions. In the fishbowl example, students generated a substantive question about producing white light with colored filters, but teachers were often unable to fully relaunch the inquiry because they felt underprepared scientifically.
finding.measure: Emergent student research questions, teacher documentation/reflection on physics inquiry, and disciplinary follow-up choices

finding.finding_summary: Although the project aimed to connect tinkering with disciplinary learning, teachers more often chose humanities, language, expression, and storytelling pathways than science-based follow-ups. The paper also notes that some classes did pursue physics experiments and hands-on activities, but this was less common and largely optional.
finding.measure: Teacher questionnaire on post-tinkering disciplinary integration choices
